source.title: Safe at One Loop, Risky at Another: Aligning Safety Across Recurrent Depths in Looped Language Models
source.authors: Yi Wang; Xiu-Yuan Qi; Dong-Qi Han; Dong-Sheng Li; Wen-Jie Wang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests jailbreak success on Ouro looped language models across recurrent inference depths, extending jailbreak robustness evaluation to a different model architecture and setting.
record.gate_note: The paper measures harmful-response attack success rates for original and jailbroken prompts. Rows below record jailbreak ASR, which bears on V4. It does not measure compliant-prefix prefilling, response-position KL, or the effect of benign fine-tuning. The text also cites prior findings about deeper recurrence and original harmful queries; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs GCG adversarial-suffix attacks (a V4 'suffix' attack) on Ouro looped models and reports harmful-response ASR next to plain harmful-query ASR for the same checkpoints. That is a new architecture and setting for V4. Its main variable is recurrent computation depth, not response-token position. AutoDAN and PAIR are prompt-rewriting jailbreaks that V4 does not name.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that plain-query ASR tends to fall with depth while jailbreak ASR can rise, with an intermediate depth worst on 2.6B. Also add that LoopDPO, which averages DPO losses over depths, does not improve on DPO. SafeBridge cuts matched, cross-depth and pooled ASR with comparable over-refusal.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates and aligns Ouro looped models across recurrent computation depths using GCG, AutoDAN, and PAIR; it does not reproduce the cited fine-tuning or response-token-depth procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies with recurrent inference depth, attack source depth, model scale, checkpoint/alignment method, and attack method. Table 5 averages attack methods and source depths; Table 2 separately reports pooled-source rates by attack method.

fits_no_version.finding: Jailbreak and plain-query ASR vary strongly with recurrent inference depth. Attacks built against one recurrent depth transfer to others. Averaged jailbreak ASR is sometimes below plain-query ASR for aligned checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In looped LMs, safety differs across recurrent computation depths and jailbreaks transfer across depths; this axis is distinct from response-token position.

record.code_released: The authors state that code and model checkpoints will be released upon acceptance; no URL is stated.
record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the ASR results. It generates one response per query and inference depth using greedy decoding and uses the HarmBench classifier to judge harmfulness. ASR averages in Table 5 obscure attack-method and source-depth differences; Table 2 and the transfer analyses provide some separate attack-method or source-depth results.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit is reached. Omitted additional attack results include Table 1's original, matched, cross-depth, and overall aggregates; Table 2 pooled-source results for Vanilla, SFT, SafeDPO, and LoopDPO; Figure 4's individual source-depth × inference-depth cells; and Table 4 ablation ASRs. Priority was given to all per-inference-depth ASRs in Table 5 and pooled-source results for DPO and SafeBridge by attack method in Table 2.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start and decoding changes are not tested. There is no analysis of whether GCG succeeds by changing the opening response tokens.
No benign fine-tuning; SFT/DPO use safety-oriented data.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No test of whether safety is localized in parameters; the FiLM vectors are a method component.
No test of why alignment is shallow.
SafeBridge spreads safety across recurrent depths, not response-token positions.

missing.what: GCG matched and cross-depth ASR per checkpoint, alongside original-query ASR; this is the direct suffix-vs-plain comparison for V4.
Pooled GCG ASR for Vanilla (89.97/94.82), SFT, SafeDPO and LoopDPO.
Original-query ASR by inference depth, needed as the baseline for the jailbreak rows.

record.verdict_notes: Recurrent depth here is computation loops, not response-token position, so most findings do not map onto the shallow-alignment versions. The text does not say which checkpoint the attacks were optimized against. Attack sets are reused across evaluated checkpoints, so for aligned checkpoints they may be transfer attacks, which weakens the limits_scope reading. Each condition uses one greedy sample with the HarmBench classifier and no uncertainty. Vanilla Ouro's safety training is not described, though about 30% plain-query ASR suggests partial refusal. The record's baselines were systematically wrong: checkpoint comparisons, or the row's own value copied.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on a few to a few hundred harmful examples or test whether that removes refusal.
Uses safety-oriented SFT and preference-alignment datasets, not ordinary or carefully chosen benign-only fine-tuning data; it does not test benign-data-induced harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL between aligned and base models or its distribution across response positions.
Tests GCG, AutoDAN, and PAIR jailbreaks, including GCG adversarial suffixes. Does not test compliant-start prefilling or decoding changes.
SafeBridge adds depth-specific parameters, but the paper does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test whether the training data or objective causes first-token or response-position shallowness.
SafeBridge jointly trains across recurrent computation depths, but the paper does not test whether safety is spread beyond the first response tokens or whether such token-depth training holds up.

rows.subject: Ouro-1.4B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluate jailbreak responses at inference depth 1; average over attack methods and source depths.

conditions.value: 3 attack methods; 4 source depths; 4 safety benchmarks

rows.note: Jailbreak ASR averaged over the three attack methods and four source depths.
rows.check: The Table 5 jailbreak values average GCG with AutoDAN and PAIR, so the suffix effect V4 names cannot be isolated. The baselines are also wrong for V4: they compare to the Vanilla checkpoint, not to the same checkpoint's original-query ASR. Against that correct baseline, the averaged jailbreak ASR is often lower than plain-query ASR. Examples: 1.4B SFT d1 37.15→20.52, DPO d2 6.33→2.72, 2.6B SFT d4 68.76→43.69. Better recorded under fits_no_version.

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.reason: Jailbreaks produce harmful responses at substantial rates in the reported conditions; see R2-R4, R7-R9, R11-R17, R19-R20, and R25-R44. The paper also reports pooled-source success for the DPO checkpoints in R49-R51 and R55-R57.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: SafeBridge checkpoints and depth-dependent low-ASR conditions
reader_labels.reason: The attack effect is incomplete and varies by checkpoint and depth: SafeBridge has 0.98%, 1.05%, and 4.16% ASR at Ouro-1.4B depths 2–4, and 7.66%–14.13% across Ouro-2.6B depths; see R21-R24 and R45-R48. Pooled-source rates are also lower under SafeBridge than DPO in R52-R54 and R58-R60.
